transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-28
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Jared Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Samira Voss (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Horizon CTO), Ethan Ruiz (Horizon ML Eng), Lina Park (Horizon Infra), Sam Ortiz (Horizon Product)

Summary:
Quick Optimize walkthrough focused on throughput/cost simulator and KV/prefix caching playbook. Demo of the savings simulator, cost model assumptions, tradeoffs for latency vs token cost, and proposed pilot for a 3-day benchmark. Customer wants concrete numbers for a BAU query mix and confirmation around VPC/KMS controls.

Topics Covered:
- Redwood Optimize savings simulator walk-through
- Batch sizing and concurrency impact on unit cost
- Prefix/KV session caching strategies and hit-rate assumptions
- Quality tradeoffs with aggressive quantization/batching
- Security: VPC, KMS, audit logs, SSO
- Pilot scope and success criteria

Transcript:
[00:00] Jared Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, we'll go through a short demo of the Optimize savings simulator and then deep dive into a KV/prefix playbook.
[00:18] Maya Chen: Hi, Maya here. Focus for us is throughput costs — our customer-facing search and personalizations are getting expensive at peak.
[00:26] Ethan Ruiz: Yeah, main questions — can we get 20-40% token cost reduction without blowing up latency. Also need to understand cold start behavior for the session cache.
[00:34] Priya Desai: Great, that's exactly what we'll try to quantify. Quick note, transcription may flip a few terms — you might hear Redwood Optima instead of Optimize, that happens in the transcript.
[00:45] Samira Voss: I'll share my screen, loading the Optimize simulator now. Bear with me.
[00:52] [01:05] Priya Desai: Ok, on the left is the traffic profile input — we uploaded the sample trace you shared last week, Lina, thanks for that. That was about 12k requests per minute at peak in the trace.
[01:22] Lina Park: Yep that's correct, that's our US-east peak window. We also see a long tail of low-activity users.
[01:30] Priya Desai: Cool. In the middle are the model variants — we have an Llama-2-custom 30B (quantized 4-bit path), a mid-size 7B, and a cheaper 2.7B for fallback. On the right is the batching + KV config.
[01:48] Ethan Ruiz: Quick question — the Llama naming is from our side, but the emulator assumes certain kv-cache shapes. Will that matter?
[01:55] Priya Desai: We try to abstract shape via sequence length distributions. For KV we care about prefix lengths and session continuity; the simulator takes per-request prefix length histogram as input. So if your average prefix is 120 tokens vs 20 tokens, that's a big difference.
[02:12] [02:30] Jared Kim: For a baseline run we simulated your raw trace against no cache, batching at concurrency 8, and model 30B on quantized path. Cost per 1M tokens was $X in the workbook (note: placeholder in call) — with prefix KV enabled and a conservative 30% hit rate we see simulated token reduction around ~28% and effective unit cost drop ~24%.
[02:55] Maya Chen: 24% is great if latency doesn't double. What's the P50 and P95 effect?
[03:03] Priya Desai: Important point — if we allow larger batching windows to increase batching efficiency, p95 will climb. In the simulator we plotted latency vs cost: at concurrency 16 and batch-window 40ms median stays close to baseline but p95 increases by ~90ms in the sim. That's often acceptable for background personalization, not for interactive chat.
[03:28] Ethan Ruiz: So for our personalized search which needs sub-300ms p95, what's feasible?
[03:35] Priya Desai: For p95 <300ms, our config recommendation is smaller batch max (4–8) and aggressive prefix caching to reduce tokens per request — that gets most of the cost savings while keeping p95 tight. In your trace, a 35% cache hit + batch size 8 delivered ~18% cost savings and p95 stayed within 270ms in the model.
[03:58] [04:15] Samira Voss: I'm toggling the cache hit slider to show sensitivity — notice how cost savings taper off after ~50% hit; marginal returns drop because the remaining requests are cold or unique contexts.
[04:28] Lina Park: What drives hit-rate in practice? User sessionization?
[04:33] Priya Desai: Exactly — sticky session ids, user history length, and business logic that repeats prompts. If you can prefix requests with user metadata and maintain brief KV per-user state, hit rates increase. But that requires session routing or a shared cache with consistent hashing.
[04:54] Ethan Ruiz: Any guidance on storage and memory for KV? GPU memory pressure?
[04:59] Priya Desai: Good callout. KV lives on the serving node; memory for KV depends on average prefix length and number of concurrent sessions pinned. We estimate 1.2–1.8GB per 1M active sessions with average 100-token prefixes — very rough. For large-scale you want an LRU eviction policy and to shard KV across nodes. We'll include more precise numbers in the workbook.
[05:24] [05:40] Maya Chen: Security — we need KMS integration, separate keys for customer namespace, and audit logs. Can Redwood's private option support this in a VPC?
[05:49] Jared Kim: Yes, Redwood Private supports customer KMS and HSM integrations, per-tenant key material, and audit logs. For the pilot we can run dedicated capacity in your VPC or our dedicated infra with VPC peering depending on preference.
[06:06] Lina Park: Latency penalties from VPC peering?
[06:09] Priya Desai: Minimal; it's usually sub-ms to a few ms depending on region. The bigger latency impact is on cold KV misses which require recomputing prefix tokens.
[06:19] [06:35] Ethan Ruiz: Can you walk through a concrete example of the cost-sim assumptions?
[06:39] Priya Desai: Sure. Example assumption set: avg request 220 tokens, avg response 40 tokens, baseline batching at concurrency 8, token compute cost X per token for 30B quantized, network overhead Y. When enabling KV with 30% hit we subtract the avoided input tokens from compute. We also model additional overhead for KV lookup (<1ms) and slight cache warmup traffic.
[07:05] Jared Kim: We've also added a fallback policy in the sim: if a cached lookup results in low-confidence or a cache miss, route to a smaller 7B model to save cost. That routing policy in the sim led to lower tail latency in some scenarios.
[07:23] Maya Chen: Hmm, routing to smaller models worries our product team about hallucinations. How do you balance quality?
[07:30] Priya Desai: We recommend automated evals on a holdout prompt set — Redwood Optimize/evals can track answer quality per model variant and set automatic rollback thresholds. For the pilot we suggest capturing a mix of prompts and running the eval harness nightly.
[07:50] [08:05] Sam Ortiz: For success criteria we want two things: 1) 15–20% unit cost reduction net across our peak window, and 2) no more than 5% regression in core NDCG relevance metrics. Are those feasible?
[08:17] Priya Desai: That's reasonable. Our sim suggests it's in range with an aggressive prefix strategy. We'll include projected ranges in the workbook with sensitivity bounds.
[08:29] [08:45] Ethan Ruiz: Pilot mechanics — what's the minimum data we need to run a meaningful sim/pilot?
[08:52] Priya Desai: For the sim we need 24–72hrs of representative traffic traces (timestamped requests + prefix length + any session ids). For the pilot we need routing integration (API keys/service account), and a stable test endpoint — we recommend a 3-day run across a sample of users representing peak and off-peak windows.
[09:12] Jared Kim: We'll provide a pilot packet with step-by-step and a pre-configured test harness.
[09:19] [09:35] Maya Chen: On security docs — can you send SOC2 and the network diagram?
[09:39] Jared Kim: Absolutely, Lina we'll share SOC2 and our shared responsibility matrix. Also include the VPC topology examples.
[09:47] Lina Park: Thanks. For SSO we use Okta and SCIM — we'll share the IdP metadata.
[09:52] Priya Desai: Okta/SCIM is supported; we'll note any mapping quirks in the packet.
[10:00] [10:18] Samira Voss: Switching back to the simulator, I'm going to turn on a quantization tolerance slider — if you push to more aggressive quantization (3-bit or custom kernels) you see cost drop but some answer laxity appears on sensitive prompts. We flagged that in the sim as quality risk.
[10:35] Ethan Ruiz: Is custom quantization something Redwood will recommend?
[10:39] Priya Desai: We recommend model-level testing before production. For many workloads 4-bit quantization is a sweet spot. We can help with a micro-benchmark to validate accuracy for your prompt set.
[10:54] [11:10] Jared Kim: Ok now the playbook section — we've distilled a 4-step KV/prefix playbook: 1) Traffic analysis + trace import, 2) Prefixing rules + sessionization, 3) Conservative pilot with 3-day run and monitoring dashboards, 4) Rollout with progressive canary and fallback to smaller models when cache miss tail grows.
[11:33] Maya Chen: Step 2 — prefixing rules — are those library changes on our side or middleware?
[11:38] Priya Desai: Usually a small middleware shim or routing layer that attaches user state and canonicalizes prompts. Might be server-side in your gateway. We provide examples in Node/Python.
[11:50] Ethan Ruiz: Any gotchas with prompt canonicalization?
[11:54] Priya Desai: Watch out for personal data in prefixes — PII needs special handling/PII scrub before caching. Also canonicalization must avoid changing intent.
[12:08] [12:25] Samira Voss: Jumping to the dashboard — here are the Optimize dashboards we'll surface: token-level cost by route, cache hit heatmaps by hour, p95 latency overlays, and model downgrade alerts. You'll be able to export the workbook at any time.
[12:42] Maya Chen: Can we get per-customer cost allocation? Very important for our billing.
[12:47] Jared Kim: Yes, cost attribution per API key or tenant is available in the console.
[12:52] [13:10] Ethan Ruiz: How deterministic are the sim numbers? We want credible ranges for exec review.
[13:16] Priya Desai: The simulator provides median projections and 90% uncertainty bands by varying hit rates, batch build-up, and cold start fraction. We always recommend treating sims as directional and running a short pilot for hard numbers.
[13:32] [13:50] Maya Chen: Would Redwood run the pilot jointly or do we run it on our infra?
[13:55] Jared Kim: Both options. For faster results we can run it on Redwood Dedicated or our hosted API with data residency controls; for strict compliance you might prefer Redwood Private in your VPC. We'll propose options in the packet.
[14:12] [14:30] Sam Ortiz: Timeline — if we start the pilot next week when could we have results?
[14:36] Priya Desai: Pilot runs 3 days plus 2 days for analysis, so about a week. If you're ready to start the week of 2026-03-30 we could have a results review early April.
[14:52] [15:10] Lina Park: Quick nit — our infra team needs expected port lists and egress rules for the pilot.
[15:15] Jared Kim: We'll include a minimal network checklist in the packet and can do a short infra call with Lina to walk through specifics.
[15:26] [15:45] Ethan Ruiz: One more question on multi-model routing — when we fallback to 7B, how do we ensure we don't change semantics?
[15:52] Priya Desai: The eval harness compares outputs across model variants on a validation set. If semantic shifts exceed thresholds we block automatic fallback and instead run the heavier model. You can configure the threshold.
[16:06] [16:25] Maya Chen: Ok that helps. Any pricing impacts from Dedicated vs Hosted for the pilot?
[16:31] Jared Kim: For a short pilot hosted costs are usually lower because no long-lived reserved capacity. Dedicated is priced as reserved capacity; for pilot we offer a short-term eval seat on Dedicated in many cases, but we'll outline pricing tradeoffs in the packet.
[16:47] [17:05] Samira Voss: Wrapping up the demo, I'll drop the cost-sim export link in the chat and the sample playbook snippets.
[17:12] Jared Kim: Great. Quick recap of next steps: Jared will share the workbook and security docs; Priya will produce a pilot test plan and kick off the run; Lina will provide traces and IdP details. Follow-up call to review pilot results week of 2026-04-06.
[17:34] Maya Chen: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[17:38] Ethan Ruiz: Thanks.
[17:40] Lina Park: Thank you.
[17:43] Jared Kim: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links. Bye.

End of meeting.

Notes on transcript quality: Medium — multiple speakers, a few transcription glitches (product names, minor mis-attributions).
